transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. Chat. What brings you in today?

Well, Dr. Chat, my family made me come down here. They brought me in because of what happened at the county fair. I was supposed to be giving a talk, but I ended up climbing right up onto the tractor... it was one of those newer models, a big John Deere. My daddy always said if it ain't green, it ain't worth the diesel it drinks. We had a red one once, an old Farmall, back in '82 I think, but the transmission blew out right in the middle of the corn harvest. Cost us an absolute fortune to haul it out of the mud. 

Anyway, I was up on the tractor during my talk, and I kept jerking the controls, pulling the levers back and forth to show the crowd the 'new pattern.' It's a very important pattern, you see. But the soil out by our south pasture has been way too alkaline lately anyway. I told my brother we need more sulfur, but he never listens. He's always been stubborn, even when we were kids catching frogs out by the creek behind the old silo. 

But yeah, at the fair, I just... I couldn't make myself stop jerking the controls to show them the pattern. People were yelling at me to get down, hollering real loud, but I just couldn't stop doing it. So... they drove me here.
Have you been sleeping much less than usual without feeling tired?

Well, sleep... sleep is a funny thing lately. Most nights I might catch two, maybe three hours at best, just dozing in my old recliner. But then I'm up before the sun even thinks about rising, feeling completely charged up, ready to work the whole place like I slept a full eight hours. Which is good, because there's always so much to do. You know, that recliner used to belong to my uncle Roy. He bought it at a Sears Roebuck back in '95. Brown corduroy, ugly as sin, but comfortable. Uncle Roy used to sit in that chair and carve these little wooden ducks out of scrap pine. He gave me one once, painted it with this bright green head like a mallard, but the paint chipped off after a few years because he didn't seal it right. I told him he needed a good polyurethane, but he was just like my brother, never listened to a word I said. Anyway, yeah, I just don't need much rest these days, I'm just ready to go.
When you were jerking the tractor controls, were you trying to relieve a distressing thought or fear that kept bothering you?

No, no, it wasn't like a fear or nothing like that. I wasn't trying to stop a bad thought. I just... I had to show them the pattern. It's the new pattern for the fields. You see, the way we've been plowing for the last fifty years, it's all wrong. It disturbs the topsoil too much. My granddaddy, he used to plow deep, real deep. He had this old mule named Buster. Meanest mule you ever did see. Buster would kick you soon as look at you if you walked behind him without whistling first. Granddaddy said you always gotta let a mule know you're there. He lost half his left pinky finger to a snapping turtle once, down by the creek, but that's neither here nor there. But yeah, the pattern... it's about the energy lines in the earth. If you don't line up the furrows with the magnetic north, the crops just don't yield right. I was just trying to show them how the levers have to move to follow the lines.
Do you feel that these ideas about the fields and patterns are especially important or special, beyond what other people would think?

Well, sure they are. I mean, I know for a fact I'm the only farmer in this whole county who can actually prove this entire new way of growing. It's revolutionary, really. The folks over at the university extension, the lenders at the bank... they all ought to be listening to me and taking notes instead of doubting me all the time. 

But you know how lenders are. Old man Henderson down at the First National, he always sits behind that big mahogany desk of his, wearing these cheap clip-on ties. I told him once, I said, 'Henderson, a real man ties his own knot.' He didn't like that much. Just stared at me over those thick bifocals. He gets his glasses at the same optometrist my wife used to go to, Dr. Miller over in town. Miller had this huge saltwater fish tank right in the waiting room. Had a pufferfish in there that would just float in the corner, staring at the bubbles. I always wondered what a fish like that thinks about all day, just swimming in a glass box. Probably gets bored out of its mind. We had a dog that got bored once, a blue heeler named Rusty, chewed straight through the screen door on the back porch because a squirrel was sitting on the railing taunting him...
When you find yourself doing the repetitive behavior, do you also have unwanted, distressing thoughts that you feel driven to neutralize?

No, I don't... I don't have bad thoughts like that. It's just the pattern, like I said. The tractor levers just need to move that way. I'm not trying to stop anything bad from happening in my head. It's just... well, it's just the way it has to be done now. 

You know, speaking of tractors, my first one was an old International Harvester. Bright red. Got it at an auction over in Miller County back in '82. The auctioneer was this fellow named Earl, talked so fast you'd think his tongue was on a motor. Earl used to wear these big silver belt buckles with turquoise stones in 'em. Said he bought 'em off a Navajo fella out in New Mexico when he was driving a long-haul rig. I always wanted to drive a big rig, just get out on the open road and see the country. Out west, where the sky is just... huge. My cousin went out to Wyoming once to work on a cattle ranch. Said the wind blew so hard it would take the hat right off your head and you'd never see it again. He lost a good Stetson that way. Cost him over a hundred dollars. I wouldn't pay a hundred dollars for a hat, not unless it was made of gold...
Do you feel driven to do this because of a recurring intrusive thought that you try to prevent or neutralize?

Doc, I feel like a stuck belt on a John Deere the way we keep going over this. Like I said, no, there ain't no recurring thought I'm trying to fight off. I'm not preventing nothing. It's just the way the levers gotta move for the earth's energy. 

But speaking of stuck belts, I had this neighbor, Tom Higgins, who lost his whole index finger trying to fix a fan belt while the engine was still running. Just snipped it right off. Tom was a stubborn old bird. He actually put the severed finger in a thermos of ice water and drove himself to the hospital in his pickup. It was a '78 Ford F-150, two-tone, brown and tan. They don't make trucks like that anymore. Now everything's got computers in it. You can't even change the oil without a computer telling you it's okay. I remember when a man could fix his own engine with just a socket wrench and a little elbow grease. My dad had this whole set of Craftsman wrenches, the old ones made in America, before they started shipping all the manufacturing overseas. He kept them in this heavy red metal toolbox that weighed about fifty pounds even when it was empty. Used to sit right on the workbench next to this old coffee tin full of rusty nails...
Do you feel anxious or tense before you do the repetitive action, and then briefly relieved afterward?

Well, anxious... no, not really anxious. I don't get tense about it. It's just a thing I do with the levers, like I said. There's no big buildup of tension or relief or anything like that. It's just part of the process. 

Process is important, you know? Like when you're canning tomatoes. My grandmother used to can tomatoes every August. Her kitchen would be so hot, steam everywhere, smelled like basil and hot glass. She had these huge Mason jars, the old ones with the zinc lids and rubber rings. You had to get the seal just right or the whole batch would spoil. She'd line them all up on the counter, probably fifty jars at a time. Used to grow her own tomatoes, too—Big Boys and Early Girls. She had a garden out back that was mostly just clay and rocks, but she could grow anything. She used to say the secret was eggshells and coffee grounds. My grandfather drank his coffee black as tar, boiled it on the stove in this blue enamel percolator. That percolator had a little glass knob on the top, and I used to watch the coffee bubble up into it. It sounded like a heartbeat, just thumping away on the burner. He got that percolator at a hardware store that used to be right on Main Street, before the big box stores moved in and ran everyone out of business...
Have you been feeling unusually high, euphoric, or overly confident most of the day?

Well, yeah, sometimes. Some mornings I wake up and I feel like the whole valley is just opening up for me, you know? I'll be out on the porch, grinning at absolutely nothing, feeling like I could run the whole county single-handed. But then, if one of the hired hands questions how I want the feed loaded, or if my wife tells me I need to slow down, I just snap. I get so mad, like they've insulted the family name or something. 

My family name goes way back in this county, by the way. My great-grandfather settled here before the railroad even came through. He built the original farmhouse with timber he cut himself. Used a two-man crosscut saw. I still have that saw hanging in the barn. It's got these wooden handles that are worn completely smooth from all the sweat and friction. You look at a tool like that, and you think about the sheer muscle it took to build a life back then. No power tools, no electricity. Just men and mules. We had a mule named Buster when I was a boy. Meanest animal you ever met. He'd kick you as soon as look at you. My dad used to say Buster had a heart of pure coal. We mostly used him for pulling stumps, because he was too ornery to hitch to a plow. Ploughs are completely different now, anyway. You get these massive John Deere rigs with GPS in the cab. You can practically take a nap while the tractor drives itself. I don't trust it, though. A man ought to have his hands on the wheel, feeling the dirt...
Do you ever feel that something terrible will happen unless you do the lever movement exactly right?

No, no, I don't feel like anything terrible is gonna happen. It's not like a life or death thing. It's just... it's just the way the levers gotta go, like I said. Nothing bad is gonna fall out of the sky if I don't do it. 

Speaking of the sky, we had the worst hail storm I've ever seen back in '98. Hailstones the size of golf balls just pummeling the roof. Sounded like a thousand men beating on the tin with hammers. It completely flattened the winter wheat. Ruined the whole crop in about fifteen minutes. My neighbor, old man Jenkins, he tried to run out and cover his prize tomato plants with a tarp and got clocked right on the forehead with a piece of ice. Left a welt the size of a turkey egg. He had to wear a hat pulled down low for a month so folks wouldn't stare at church. He went to the First Baptist over on Elm Street. The one with the big white steeple. They repainted that steeple a few years back, but they used the wrong kind of primer, and it started peeling before Thanksgiving. You gotta use a good oil-based primer if you want paint to stick to wood that's been out in the weather that long. People just don't know how to do a job right anymore. They want everything done fast, cheap. Like those prefabricated barns they sell now. Slap 'em together in a day, and the first stiff wind comes along and blows the roof right off into the next county...
